clue.text: Hostilities and malice in the navy

parts.note: hostilities between nations amount to war
malice is spite, a wish to hurt

explanation.surface: Fighting and ill will are rife among the sailors of the fleet.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: HMS WARSPITE was a famous Royal Navy battleship, so the name is one found in the navy.
explanation.definitionFit: A celebrated British battleship bore this name, so it is a vessel serving in the fleet.

clue.text: Method — go off with transit permit

parts.note: a way of doing something is a method
to go off is to leave

explanation.surface: A procedure for departing that comes with a travel pass.
explanation.walkthrough: A WAYLEAVE is a British legal term for a right of way granted over someone's land, for example to run cables or a path.
explanation.definitionFit: A legal grant of passage across private land is a permit allowing transit over it.

explanation.surface: Describing how a satellite travels out and returns.
explanation.definitionFit: A satellite's orbit carries it all the way about the planet, and a journey out and home again is the everyday travel sense.

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece written on top of another comes first

parts.note: P is simply a letter of the alphabet
GBS are the initials of the playwright George Bernard Shaw

explanation.surface: A scornful letter written about the playwright George Bernard Shaw.
explanation.walkthrough: The interjection PSHAW is uttered to show contempt, hence 'utterly' contemptuous: it is a word you utter.
explanation.definitionFit: This exclamation is an old-fashioned spoken expression of scorn or impatience.

clue.text: What a chest for a well-grown lad !

definitions.text: What a chest for a well-grown lad !

parts.words: What a chest for a well-grown lad
parts.note: a high chest of drawers is named as if it were meant for a tall young fellow

explanation.surface: Admiring the broad chest of a strapping youth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chest' looks like part of the body, but it is the furniture: a TALLBOY is a tall chest of drawers, and a well-grown lad is a tall boy.
explanation.definitionFit: This furniture word names a high chest of drawers, literally a lanky youngster.

explanation.surface: Someone unmoved by all this disruption.
explanation.definitionFit: Something stationary is not moving, and crackle on a radio set is called atmospheric noise of this kind.

clue.text: Harness of the efficient old ratcatcher ?

explanation.surface: The gear belonging to a skilled old rodent catcher.
explanation.walkthrough: Trappings were the ornamental harness of a horse; read as 'trap-pings', they are the sounds of traps going off, which an efficient ratcatcher would hear often.
explanation.definitionFit: Ceremonial horse gear is the first sense; the second hears traps snapping shut busily for a successful rodent catcher.

explanation.surface: A small spoonful of honey is the sensible choice.
explanation.definitionFit: A small sample of food is a mouthful to try, and one of the five senses is the palate's.

indicators.note: staging something reworks it, so these letters are produced again in a new order

explanation.surface: A playwright's rule book for putting on shows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of theatrical production' rearranges MY CODE, and the result is itself a kind of theatrical production.
explanation.definitionFit: A light-hearted play is a classic form of stage drama.

clue.text: A rotten article from a place in Persia

parts.note: rotten food is bad
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A decayed object brought back from somewhere in Iran.
explanation.definitionFit: Abadan is an oil-refining city in southwest Iran, the country once called Persia.

parts.note: a cudgel belonging to a teenager, and also a social group for teenagers

explanation.surface: Asking what weapon teenage gangs carry.
explanation.walkthrough: A club is both a weapon and a society, and a youth is an adolescent: the weapon reading is the false trail.
explanation.definitionFit: Organisations providing leisure activities for teenagers are named with a word for a cudgel.

clue.text: Land in Asia, like Dr Johnson

parts.note: as means like, in 'as good as gold'
Samuel Johnson, the dictionary maker, was known as Sam

explanation.surface: A country in Asia compared with the great lexicographer.
explanation.walkthrough: ASSAM is a state in northeast India, famous for its tea.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a region of northeastern India, a territory on the Asian continent.

clue.text: Make a gift to Woden, maybe

indicators.note: maybe suggests the name is only one possible arrangement of these letters

explanation.surface: Offering a present to the Norse god Woden.
explanation.definitionFit: To bestow money or property on an institution is to give it funds.

clue.text: Feast in the dorm? Take cover

explanation.surface: A midnight feast in a school dormitory, and someone told to hide.
explanation.walkthrough: A spread is a feast, so a feast laid out on the beds in a dormitory is a bed spread.
explanation.definitionFit: A decorative blanket over a bed is its top layer, and a meal laid out on a bed is a dormitory banquet.

parts.note: the proverb calls this quality the spice of life, and vital means of life

explanation.surface: A seasoning claimed to be essential.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spice' looks like a kitchen ingredient, but the proverb says 'variety is the spice of life', so it is the spice said to be 'of life', vital.
explanation.definitionFit: Diversity is the quality the old saying calls the spice of life.

parts.note: turning liquid into vapour, read like a business instruction

explanation.surface: An order to switch a household over to gas supply.
explanation.walkthrough: It reads like changing a home's fuel to gas, but it means turning a liquid into vapour.
explanation.definitionFit: Turning from liquid into vapour is passing into a gaseous state.

clue.text: No French period for the minority

parts.note: non is French for no
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: A French refusal to set aside time for minorities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minority' here is the legal state of being under age, not a smaller group.
explanation.definitionFit: Being legally under age is called one's minority, the youthful years before adulthood.

clue.text: Thousand dollar bet made by Richardson's hero.

parts.note: a grand is slang for a thousand dollars
once a bet is made, it is on

explanation.surface: A big wager placed by a novelist's leading man.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Charles GRANDISON is the hero of Samuel Richardson's 1753 novel of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Richardson's novel takes its title from its virtuous protagonist, Sir Charles.

explanation.surface: A support with legs spread apart.
explanation.walkthrough: In gunnery, to bracket a target is to fire shots either side of it, also called straddling.
explanation.definitionFit: Artillery fire landing on both sides of a target brackets it, and sitting with legs apart over something is the other sense.

clue.text: Chop I ate finally to relieve pangs

indicators.note: finally points to the closing stretch of these words, where the letters sit

explanation.surface: A diner who finally ate the chop to ease hunger pangs.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run at the end of 'cHOP I ATE', which is what 'finally' signals.
explanation.definitionFit: A drug derived from the poppy is something taken to dull pain.

parts.note: the canon is the accepted list of books of the Bible, whose second is about leaving Egypt

explanation.surface: A clergyman's follow-up publication.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Canon' looks like a clergyman, but it is the biblical canon, whose second book follows Genesis.
explanation.definitionFit: The second book of the Old Testament tells of the Israelites leaving Egypt.

parts.words: The brave music of a —— drum
parts.note: a line from FitzGerald's version of the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, with one word left blank

explanation.surface: A line of poetry quoted with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is from Edward FitzGerald's Rubaiyat: 'Ah, take the Cash, and let the Credit go, Nor heed the rumble of a distant Drum!' and its earlier version 'the brave Music of a distant Drum'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word describes a drum heard far off, remote from the listener.

parts.note: pupils who live at home rather than boarding at school

explanation.surface: Students who prefer studying at home.
explanation.walkthrough: At a British boarding school, pupils who attend by day and sleep at home are called day boys.
explanation.definitionFit: Non-boarding pupils at a residential school go home each evening.

indicators.note: madly suggests the letters are thrown into wild disorder

explanation.surface: A village chief who rioted wildly.
explanation.walkthrough: 25 down is PAPER, so the head man of a newspaper is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: The person in charge of a newspaper decides what it prints.

parts.note: separating the sheep from the goats is a split into two groups, and -otomy sounds like a surgical cut

explanation.surface: A procedure carried out on farm animals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Operation' suggests surgery, and the word ends like one (-tomy, cutting), but it is the biblical separating of sheep from goats: a division into two.
explanation.definitionFit: A division into two contrasting parts is what separating the flock does.

clue.text: Stick your neck out as weight-lifter

explanation.surface: An invitation to take a risk, like a weightlifting athlete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick your neck out' is an idiom for taking a risk, but here it is literal: stretching the neck to see.
explanation.definitionFit: Stretching the neck to look is the verb sense, and a machine for hoisting heavy loads is the other.

parts.note: the shrew of Shakespeare's comedy lived in this Italian city

explanation.surface: Asking where a woman named Katharina became cross.
explanation.walkthrough: Katharina is the shrew in Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew, which is set in Padua.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare sets his shrew comedy in this northern Italian university city.

parts.note: a Chinese saying calls a threat that is all show a harmless tiger made of flimsy stuff

explanation.surface: Big cats that hold no terror in China.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paper tiger', from a Chinese expression popularised by Mao, means something that looks fearsome but is harmless.
explanation.definitionFit: A threat that is fearsome only in appearance is called a tiger made of this flimsy material.

clue.text: A decoration goes to one's head

definitions.text: A decoration goes to one's head

parts.words: A decoration goes to one's head
parts.note: an honour that makes one conceited, read as an ornament worn on the head

explanation.surface: Someone whose medal has made them vain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes to one's head' suggests vanity, but the decoration is worn literally on the head.
explanation.definitionFit: A jewelled crown-like band is an ornament worn on top of the head.

parts.note: a candidate with no rival is elected without any poll, so no votes are cast

explanation.surface: A hopeless candidate in an election.
explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a candidate who loses badly, but one standing with no rival is returned without a vote.
explanation.definitionFit: A candidate facing no rival needs no ballot, being returned without contest.

clue.text: Ladybirds of singular appearance on the Canterbury road

definitions.text: of singular appearance on the Canterbury road

explanation.surface: Ladybird beetles looking odd on the road to Canterbury.
explanation.walkthrough: A reeve is the female of the ruff, a wading bird, so reeves are lady birds; the Reeve is one of Chaucer's Canterbury pilgrims, appearing singly.
explanation.definitionFit: Females of the ruff wader are lady birds, and a single estate steward rides among Chaucer's pilgrims to Canterbury.

indicators.note: perhaps suggests these letters could also be arranged some other way

explanation.surface: Wondering whether angering a holy person would push them away.
explanation.definitionFit: To make someone unfriendly or distant is to drive them away from former affection.
